questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how the structure of a eukaryotic cell allows it to carry out protein synthesis efficiently. (3)
hints: Name the organelles involved in genetic information and protein production.
Link each organelle to its function.
questions.solution:
The nucleus contains the genetic information / DNA coding for proteins. [B1]
Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis. [B1]
Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration to support cell processes. [B1]

questions.prompt: A microscope image of a cell is 36 mm long. The actual cell is 60 micrometres long. Calculate the magnification. (3)
hints: Make the units the same first.
Use magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
questions.solution:
Convert 36 mm to 36 000 micrometres. [B1]
Use magnification = image size / actual size. [B1]
Magnification = 36 000 / 60 = 600. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Describe a method to investigate osmosis in cylinders of potato tissue and explain how the results would show the concentration at which there is no net movement of water. (4)
hints: Control the size of the cylinders and the time in solution.
Think about what zero change in mass means.
questions.solution:
Cut equal-sized potato cylinders and record their initial mass. [B1]
Place them in a range of known sugar or salt concentrations for the same time. [B1]
Remove, blot dry and measure the final mass, then calculate change or percentage change. [B1]
The concentration giving zero change in mass is the isotonic concentration / has the same water potential as the potato cells. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain one medical use of stem cells and one risk or limitation associated with their use. (3)
hints: What makes a stem cell different from a specialised cell?
Give one benefit and one drawback.
questions.solution:
Stem cells can differentiate into specialised cells to replace damaged tissue. [B1]
They may be used to treat conditions such as paralysis or diabetes by replacing non-functioning cells. [B1]
A risk is rejection, infection, tumour formation or ethical concern depending on the source. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport. (4)
hints: State the direction of movement for each process.
Which process needs energy?
questions.solution:
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration. [B1]
Osmosis is the net movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution. [B1]
Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient and requires energy from respiration. [B1]
All three move substances across cell membranes. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how the structure of the small intestine is adapted for efficient absorption of digested food molecules. (4)
hints: Think about surface area, diffusion distance and blood flow.
Some nutrients need active transport.
questions.solution:
Villi and microvilli provide a large surface area. [B1]
The epithelium is one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance. [B1]
A good blood supply maintains a steep concentration gradient. [B1]
Cells contain many mitochondria to provide energy for active transport where needed. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how the heart and blood vessels work together to supply respiring cells with oxygen. (4)
hints: Follow the route from heart to tissue and back.
Relate vessel structure to function.
questions.solution:
The heart contracts to create pressure and pump blood. [B1]
Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. [B1]
Capillaries have thin walls for diffusion of oxygen into tissues. [B1]
Veins return blood to the heart and valves help prevent backflow. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Describe how you could investigate the effect of pH on the activity of amylase. (4)
hints: Iodine tests for starch.
Only pH should change between trials.
questions.solution:
Use amylase and starch with buffer solutions of different pH values. [B1]
Keep temperature, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration constant. [B1]
At regular intervals test samples with iodine for remaining starch. [B1]
Record the time for starch to disappear and compare rate, for example using 1/time. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how coronary heart disease can develop and give one treatment that can reduce its effects. (4)
hints: Which blood vessels feed the heart muscle?
Link narrowing to oxygen supply.
questions.solution:
Fatty material can build up in coronary arteries. [B1]
The lumen narrows, reducing blood flow and oxygen delivery to heart muscle. [B1]
This can cause angina or a heart attack. [B1]
A stent can keep the artery open, or statins can reduce blood cholesterol. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Compare xylem and phloem tissues in plants. (4)
hints: One tissue mainly moves water; the other moves sugars.
Include one structural difference.
questions.solution:
Xylem transports water and mineral ions from roots through the plant. [B1]
Xylem vessels are dead, hollow and strengthened with lignin. [B1]
Phloem transports dissolved sugars by translocation. [B1]
Phloem contains living cells and transport can occur to sources and sinks in different directions. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how vaccination can reduce the spread of an infectious disease through a population. (4)
hints: Use the words antigen, antibody and memory cell.
Think about both the individual and the population.
questions.solution:
A vaccine introduces antigens from a pathogen in a safe form. [B1]
Lymphocytes produce specific antibodies and memory cells. [B1]
On later infection the secondary immune response is faster and produces more antibodies. [B1]
If many people are immune, transmission is reduced because fewer susceptible hosts are available. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain why antibiotics can treat some infectious diseases but not others. (3)
hints: What type of pathogen do antibiotics target?
Viruses use host-cell machinery.
questions.solution:
Antibiotics kill bacteria or inhibit bacterial growth. [B1]
Viruses reproduce inside host cells and do not have the bacterial targets that antibiotics act on. [B1]
Therefore antibiotics do not cure viral diseases. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Describe how the body prevents pathogens from entering and responds if they do enter. (4)
hints: Start with barriers at body surfaces.
Then consider white blood cells.
questions.solution:
Skin forms a physical barrier and produces antimicrobial secretions. [B1]
Mucus and cilia in the respiratory tract trap and move pathogens away. [B1]
White blood cells can engulf pathogens by phagocytosis. [B1]
Lymphocytes produce antibodies and antitoxins. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how monoclonal antibodies are produced and give one use. (4)
hints: Hybridoma cells combine two useful properties.
State one application.
questions.solution:
A mouse is exposed to an antigen so lymphocytes producing the required antibody are formed. [B1]
The lymphocytes are fused with tumour cells to make hybridoma cells. [B1]
A selected hybridoma clone divides and produces large quantities of one antibody. [B1]
Monoclonal antibodies can be used in pregnancy tests, diagnostics, measurements or targeted treatments. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Describe two ways a farmer could reduce the spread of plant disease and explain why each works. (4)
hints: Think about reservoirs, vectors and transmission routes.
Explain the mechanism, not just the action.
questions.solution:
Remove and destroy infected plants to reduce the reservoir of pathogens. [B1]
Use resistant varieties so infection is less likely to establish or cause damage. [B1]
Control vectors such as insects to reduce transmission. [B1]
Disinfect tools to prevent transfer between plants. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain how changing temperature can affect the rate of decomposition in an ecosystem. (3)
hints: Decomposition depends on microorganisms and enzymes.
Think about an optimum temperature.
questions.solution:
At low temperature decomposer enzyme reactions are slow. [B1]
As temperature rises towards an optimum, enzyme activity and respiration increase so decomposition is faster. [B1]
At very high temperatures enzymes can denature and decomposer activity falls. [B1]

questions.prompt: A student is answering an AQA-style practice question. Explain two ways human activity can reduce biodiversity and one way conservation can help protect it. (3)
hints: Give a mechanism for each human impact.
Then give one conservation action.
questions.solution:
Habitat destruction reduces the number and variety of organisms that can survive. [B1]
Pollution or climate change can alter conditions and eliminate sensitive species. [B1]
Conservation can protect habitats/species, restore ecosystems, use breeding programmes or reduce damaging activity. [B1]
